Welcome to SquatClient, a graphical client for MUDs, MUSHes and other MU games. It remembers your worlds, keeps full-colour scrollback, lets you automate things with a TinyFugue-style scripting language or Lua, and can keep your connections alive while the app is closed.
This help is built into the app. It works offline and everything in it is searchable.
Want to connect to a game? See Connecting and worlds.
Want your connections to survive closing the app? See Squatter.
Looking for a key? See Keyboard shortcuts.
Want to automate things with triggers and macros? Start with the scripting language, then Lua scripting.
Unsure what a word means? See the Glossary.

A squatter is a saved remote relay: a squatterd you run on a server, or a TinyFugue (TinyFugue as a squatter). You can save many squatters, for example home-vps and work-box.
Each world chooses how it connects with its Connect via setting:
Direct: straight from this computer to the game. The connection ends when the app closes.
A saved squatter: the squatter holds the game connection. It survives closing the app, and when you come back everything you missed is replayed.
Different worlds can use different squatters, and some can be direct, all at the same time.
There is one hop for now: SquatClient, then the squatter, then the game. Chaining squatters, or a squatter that goes out through a proxy, is not available yet.

Then add the squatter in SquatClient as host 127.0.0.1, port 10327. On the server, start squatterd with --bind 127.0.0.1 --insecure-loopback: it then accepts only connections from the server itself, which is safe because the ssh tunnel already encrypts everything.

A world is a saved connection to a game. Open the world manager with Ctrl-O (Cmd-O on macOS), the menu (Session, Worlds) or the button in the tab bar. Select a world and press Connect, or double-click it. Worlds are stored in your SquatClient configuration folder. Passwords are not: they go to your operating system's keychain.
Group optional folder name used to group the list
Host and Port where the game listens
Connect via Direct (from this computer; ends when the app closes) or a saved squatter that holds the connection for you; see Squatters and routing
Encoding how text from the game is decoded: UTF-8 (default) or Latin-1
Skip certificate verification accept any certificate; only for games with a self-signed certificate
Connect automatically connect when the app starts
Login template text sent after connecting; {name} and {password} are filled in for you
Password replaces {password}; stored in the OS keychain

Tick Use TLS when the game offers an encrypted port. Certificates are checked strictly by default. Some games use a self-signed certificate; for those, tick Skip certificate verification. That removes the protection against someone impersonating the game, so only use it for games you trust.

UTF-8 is the default. It handles accented letters, emoji and box-drawing characters. Some older games send Latin-1; if accents look garbled, switch that world to Latin-1. You can set the default for new connections in Settings.
If a world has a login template, SquatClient sends it for you after connecting. A typical MUSH template is:

Game passwords are saved in the operating system keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service on Linux), never in the worlds file. The file only records that a password exists. If the keychain cannot be reached, connecting to a world that needs a password fails with an error instead of sending an empty password.

A squatter never stores your game passwords either: your client sends the login every time. Lines that look like logins or password changes are masked on screen and never saved in history; see Passwords.

Each connection is a tab. Press Alt-1 to Alt-9 to switch, or Ctrl-Tab and Ctrl-Shift-Tab to cycle. A badge on a tab counts unread lines in background connections, and the status bar shows how many are active. Closing a tab disconnects it. A connection that has ended stays in its tab until you dismiss it, showing the reason and the last text received.
Scripts can also define and connect worlds; see /addworld, /connect, /world and /fg in Commands.
To keep a connection running while the app is closed, read Squatter. If a connection fails, see Troubleshooting.

If you already run TinyFugue (TF) on a server, it can act as your squatter. You see all of its connections in SquatClient, read their history and type into them, while TinyFugue keeps running its own triggers and macros.
In TinyFugue (built with the squat support) run /squat start, then /squat pair. It prints a one-time pairing code and its fingerprint.
In SquatClient open the Squatters dialog, choose Add a squatter, set Type to TinyFugue, and enter the host, the port (10328 unless you changed it) and the code.
Compare the fingerprint, then press Trust and pair.
A TinyFugue squatter and a squatterd use different ports and different protocol paths. If you pick the wrong Type, SquatClient says so and nothing is sent to the server.
Every TinyFugue connection shows a badge on its tab and a Keyboard control in the status bar:
Type too both of you TinyFugue
Take the keyboard only SquatClient TinyFugue
Take over fully only SquatClient SquatClient

While TinyFugue keeps the keyboard, the input line is disabled and says so. If TinyFugue is set to ask first (squattakeover=ask), the change waits until its user allows it and you see a message meanwhile.

Triggers run in only one place at a time, so nothing fires twice. By default TinyFugue runs them and SquatClient only shows the result. In the Squatters dialog you can choose this app (while connected): SquatClient then takes over triggers whenever it is connected and TinyFugue gets them back when you leave.
Lines you did not type are marked in the output: [tf] for TinyFugue's own keyboard and [remote] for another device.
A world whose Connect via is a TinyFugue squatter is a world record in TinyFugue, and the two are kept in agreement both ways:

Save, rename or delete it here and TinyFugue's record is created, renamed or deleted (and saved with /saveworld, so it survives a restart). Credentials are never copied: this app logs in with its own saved password, unless the record in TinyFugue has its own login.
Rename it in TinyFugue (or add, delete or change one at its keyboard) and the tab, this app's world and the world lists here follow.
Connecting goes by that record, so the tab, the world and TinyFugue all carry the same name.
Rename a tab (right-click the tab, Rename (in TinyFugue)…) and the world is renamed in TinyFugue, here, and on the tab.

A connection you opened by address (not from a world) is only a temporary world in TinyFugue, (unnamed1) and the like. Right-click its tab and choose Save as a world in TinyFugue…: it becomes a named world in TinyFugue (kept after the connection closes) and in your list, and the tab follows. In TinyFugue itself the same is /renameworld <name>.
Tabs of connections that run through TinyFugue end in an orange (tf); hover a tab to see which squatter holds the connection.

Press Worlds… next to a TinyFugue squatter to see, add, edit, delete and connect TinyFugue's own world records. Passwords are write-only: they are stored in TinyFugue and never shown or kept by SquatClient. TinyFugue logs in by itself, so SquatClient sends nothing for the login. A viewer device can look and connect but not edit.

Press Scripts… (admin devices) to send a TinyFugue macro file to TinyFugue and activate it there: pick a file or paste the text, name it (letters, digits, . -, ending in .tf) and press Send and load. Sending the same name again replaces the script and loads it again.
What the script may do is decided in TinyFugue, by squatscripts:

safe the script runs sandboxed: no shell (/sh, /quote !), no files, no new connections, no Lua, and it cannot change TinyFugue's squat settings or its restriction level. The same holds whenever one of its triggers or macros fires later
on the script runs with TinyFugue's own rights, like a file you loaded yourself
Use safe unless you wrote the script. Deleting a script removes only the file: triggers it already defined stay until you undefine them or TinyFugue restarts.
Lines TinyFugue gagged are hidden by default. Settings → Show lines TinyFugue gagged shows them, marked as gagged.
GMCP and MSDP data from games reaches SquatClient too, and you can send GMCP or MSDP requests to a game through TinyFugue.

What SquatClient may do depends on the role the pairing gave this device (viewer, operator or admin). Running a TinyFugue command or sending a script needs admin, and TinyFugue's squatexec / squatscripts settings must allow it.
Everything is held by TinyFugue: if it exits, its sessions end.

A squatter keeps your game connections running while SquatClient is closed. It is a small separate program, squatterd, that you run on a computer that stays on, such as a home server or a cheap virtual server. Think of screen or TinyFugue on a shell account.
Already using TinyFugue on a server? It can be your squatter too: see TinyFugue as a squatter.
You close the app, and the game never notices: you stay logged in.
The squatter keeps recording what the game says. When you open SquatClient again it replays everything you missed and carries on live.
You can attach from different computers.
You do not need a squatter to use SquatClient. Without one, connections are direct and end when you quit the app.
What a squatter does not do:
It never logs in for you and stores no game passwords. SquatClient sends the login lines each time.
It never reconnects to a game by itself. If the game closes the connection, the session is shown as ended, with the reason, until you dismiss it.

SquatClient does reconnect to the squatter by itself. If your laptop sleeps or the network drops, the squatter keeps your games connected; the app reconnects to it a moment after the network is back (or the window is shown again) and catches up on everything you missed. You can turn this off in Settings, and the Squatters dialog has a Reconnect button to do it right away.
You need two things: squatterd running on the server, and SquatClient paired with it. Pairing happens once per computer.
Get squatterd for the server from <https://github.com/itsnotyoutoday/squatClientDaemon> and start it there:

The default port is 10327, connections to it are encrypted, and its files live in ~/.squatterd. Run ./squatterd --help for the other options, for example --bind to limit the address it listens on and --data-dir to move its files.
On the server, in a second terminal, run:
It prints a one-time pairing code such as ABCD-EFGH (valid for ten minutes), the server's fingerprint, and a host and port hint.
In SquatClient open the squatters dialog (the tab-bar button), choose Add a squatter, and enter a name, the host, the port (10327 unless you changed it) and the pairing code. Press Pair.
Compare the fingerprint SquatClient shows with the one squatterd pair printed. If they are the same, press Trust and pair. If they differ, press Reject: something is between you and your server.
In the world manager set a world's Connect via to your squatter. See Squatters and routing.

The squatter makes its own encryption certificate, so no outside authority vouches for it. SquatClient therefore asks you to confirm the fingerprint once, and from then on it only talks to a server with exactly that fingerprint. If the fingerprint ever changes, the connection is refused.
Only pair computers you trust: anyone who can pair can open connections to any game from the server. ./squatterd revoke <deviceId> removes a paired computer.

Type /suspend (or /detach) to let go of your squatter sessions while leaving them running. SquatClient lets go of them, the window is minimised, and the sessions keep recording. To come back choose Resume in the Session menu (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-R); everything you missed is replayed. Closing the app has the same effect for squatter sessions.
Direct connections cannot outlive the app, so /suspend leaves them connected and just minimises the window. If you have both kinds open, only the squatter sessions are detached.

When a game closes the connection, resets it or cannot be reached, the session is ended. The tab shows the reason, the time and the last text received, and the history is kept. Choose Connect again to open a fresh connection, or Dismiss to remove the tab. Nothing reconnects by itself.
Connections to the squatter are encrypted, and the certificate is pinned when you pair.
Your computer proves who it is with a key; the squatter remembers only the public half.
Pairing codes work once and expire. Repeated wrong codes lock the sender out for five minutes.
If the squatter's port is not reachable, see Squatters and routing.
Read Squatters and routing to use several squatters, or Troubleshooting if a squatter does not respond.

Tab bar: one tab per connection, plus buttons for worlds, quick connect, squatters, search, settings and help.
Output pane: what the game says, plus your own typed lines and system messages.
Input line: where you type. Lines starting with / are commands, anything else is sent to the game.
Status bar: connection state, activity in other tabs, the pause marker, any fields your scripts add, and the clock.

Text keeps the colours and styles the game sends: bold, dim, italic, underline, strikethrough, blink and reverse. Colours can be the 16 theme colours, the 256-colour xterm palette, or 24-bit truecolour, and all of UTF-8 is displayed. Links the game marks up, and bare http:// and https:// addresses (if enabled in Settings), are clickable and open in your system browser. Only web addresses are ever opened.
Select text with the mouse and copy it as usual.
Recent output is kept in memory, up to the scrollback lines setting; older history is fetched on demand when you scroll up. Use PageUp and PageDown to scroll, or the mouse wheel.

When you scroll up, live output pauses so the text you are reading does not move (if Pause output when scrolled up is on). The status bar shows --More-- with a count of lines that arrived meanwhile. Press End (when the output has focus) or the jump button to return to live output. This takes the place of TinyFugue's --More-- prompt.

Press Cmd-F or Ctrl-Shift-F (Ctrl-F when the output has focus) to open the search bar. It offers previous and next match, case sensitivity and regular expressions, and searches the whole scrollback of the current tab.
The input line understands the Emacs editing keys TinyFugue users know. The full list is in Keyboard shortcuts. Highlights:
Home/End or Ctrl-A/Ctrl-E move to the start or end.
Ctrl-W and Alt-D delete words; Ctrl-K and Ctrl-U delete to the end or the whole line; Ctrl-Y pastes the last deletion.
Shift-Enter inserts a new line so you can write several lines before sending.
Pasting several lines sends them one by one.
Ctrl-R opens the history browser; Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-E switches to the editor.

Up and Down (or Ctrl-P and Ctrl-N) walk through lines you sent earlier. If you typed something first, only lines starting with it are offered, so typing /def and pressing Up finds your last /def command.

History is kept per world, on disk, so it survives restarts and is shared by every tab of the same world. A multi-line block is one entry. Passwords and anything typed while the game has echo off are never stored. How many entries are kept is the Command history size setting (default 20,000; see Settings).
Press Ctrl-R (or Cmd-Shift-H), or click History next to the input, to search everything you have sent to this world.
Type to filter at once. .\ switches to regular expressions and Aa to case-sensitive matching; matches are highlighted.

Up and Down select (PageUp, PageDown, Ctrl-Home, Ctrl-End jump), Enter puts the entry into the input (into the editor if it has several lines), Shift-Enter sends it now, Cmd/Ctrl-C copies it, Delete removes it, Escape closes.
Click selects, double-click loads. Clear history asks for confirmation first.

Drag the thin bar above the input upwards to make the command window taller (up to about 70% of the window); the output shrinks to match. Focus the bar and use Up and Down (PageUp and PageDown for five lines, Home for the tallest, End for the smallest). Double-click it to reset. The height is remembered.
For big pieces of code press Editor (or Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-E): the input becomes a large code editor made for MUSH softcode. It loads the first time you open it.

It colours softcode as you type (functions, [ ] { } ( ), % substitutions, #dbrefs, &ATTR and @commands, $ patterns, @@ comments), marks the matching bracket, closes ( [ { for you and underlines brackets that do not balance (the toolbar counts them).

Enter inserts a new line; Cmd/Ctrl-Enter sends the whole buffer; Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-Enter (or the Send line / selection button) sends only the selection, or the line under the cursor together with the indented lines that continue it.

Tab inserts two spaces (with a selection it indents every selected line); Shift-Tab outdents. Undo and redo (Cmd/Ctrl-Z, Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-Z or Ctrl-Y) work as in any editor. Line numbers, the line and column, and Wrap (off by default) are in the toolbar.
Cmd/Ctrl-F searches inside the editor (with replace); Escape closes that search first. The output search stays on Cmd/Ctrl-F whenever you are not in the editor.

Expand breaks long function calls over indented lines so you can read them, and Collapse puts them back; both work on the selection, or on everything when nothing is selected, and Collapse after Expand gives back exactly what you had. Keys: Cmd/Ctrl-Alt-] and Cmd/Ctrl-Alt-[.
Escape (with no search open) returns to the single line and keeps your text. Unsent text is kept as a draft for the world, across tab switches and restarts.
Pasting several lines in the editor inserts them there instead of sending them.

When you send from the editor (the whole buffer, or the selection or line) and the code has brackets that do not balance, a dialog says how many problems there are and on which lines. Fix first puts the cursor on the first problem and sends nothing; Send anyway sends it as it is. Turn the check off with Editor: ask before sending unbalanced brackets in Settings. Single-line input is never checked.
Every resulting line is sent to the game separately, in order:

Indented lines continue the previous line (setting Editor: join indented lines, on by default). A line starting with a space or tab has its leading whitespace removed and is appended directly to the line before it, with no space added, so indent freely for readability: &FN obj=[add(1, followed by 2)] is sent as &FN obj=[add(1,2)]. Add a space yourself where the code needs one.

Blank lines and lines holding only an @@ comment are dropped (setting Editor: drop blank and @@ comment lines, on by default), also between a line and its continuation. Trailing spaces are always removed.

With Delay between block lines above 0 the lines go out one per interval so a big block does not flood the game; a progress bar and a Cancel button show while it runs (lines already sent cannot be taken back).

Lines like connect name password, create name password and @password ... are recognised automatically and are never echoed, stored or logged by a squatter; the screen shows them masked (connect name ). Use /secret text for anything else you must keep out of logs.
When the game turns off echo (for a password prompt) the input becomes a masked password field with a lock icon, history is disabled and what you type is not recorded.

/upload sends a text file to the game, for example a softcode installer. Type /upload to choose the file in the system file dialog (it starts in the folder you used last; text and code files such as .txt .mush .mu .tf .lua .md are listed first, All Files is one click away), or /upload ~/code/install.mush to give the path yourself (~/ is your home folder; use quotes if the path has spaces). You can also drag a text file onto the window. Nothing is sent yet: a dialog opens first.
The dialog shows the file name, size, line count and a scrollable preview with line numbers (a second tab shows exactly what will be sent). Large files stay responsive.

It follows the same rules as multi-line mode: join continuation lines and skip blank and @@ comment lines start from your settings, and you can change them for this upload. The number of commands that will be sent is shown. Delay per line starts from your setting, or 50 ms when that is 0, so the game is not flooded; an optional prefix is put in front of every command.
The commands go to the world shown as Send to (the one in front), one line at a time. If the code has unbalanced brackets the first problems are listed and the button reads Send anyway.

While it runs you see a progress bar, the current line and the elapsed time, with Pause, Resume and Cancel. At the end a summary says how many commands were sent and skipped, or where it was cancelled. Closing the dialog while sending cancels the rest.
Command history gets one entry, /upload install.mush, not the whole file.

Only plain text files up to 5 MiB are accepted (binary files are refused with a message). UTF-8 and Latin-1 files both work; line endings are normalised. The app reads only the file you chose or typed.

Each connection has a tab. Use Alt-1 to Alt-9 or Ctrl-Tab to switch. Unread lines in background tabs show as a badge, and with desktop notifications on you also get notified. The small x on a tab disconnects it, or dismisses it if it has already ended.

Pick a theme in Settings: Dark, Light or High contrast. A theme sets the text and background colours, the 16 ANSI colours and the colours of the window chrome. You can import your own theme as JSON. If some colour combinations are hard to read, set Minimum contrast (4.5 is the WCAG AA level) and the client nudges colours to meet it. The client respects your system's reduce motion preference.

By default SquatClient shows UTF-8 text with xterm-256 and 24-bit truecolour. Type /colortest to print every colour mode (16 colours, the full 256 grid, truecolor gradients, text styles and UTF-8) and compare it with another program.

Why basic colours can differ between programs: colours 0-15 (the plain red, yellow, ... and their bright versions) are not fixed: every terminal and theme chooses its own shades, and games that use them look different in different clients. Colours 16-255 (xterm-256) and truecolour are exact everywhere. SquatClient's default dark theme uses a classic terminal palette so a game that sends basic colours looks like it does in tinyfugue; if a slot looks wrong, change it in a custom theme (see below). Bold text uses bright colours makes bold text switch to the bright variant of the 8 basic colours, as in many terminals. In scripts you can use all of these colours; see Attributes.

Dialogs trap keyboard focus and close with Escape, controls have labels, and Screen-reader mode announces new lines to assistive technology. A "Skip to input" link is the first thing a keyboard user reaches.
Learn the keys in Keyboard shortcuts, tune the client in Settings, or automate it with the scripting language. If something looks wrong, see Troubleshooting.

The Object Editor lets you work on objects and their attributes in a game as if they were files: a list of attributes on the left, a full code editor on the right, and tabs for every object you have open. It needs a connected world, because it reads and writes through the game itself.

The Object Editor is the module for MU games: PennMUSH, CobraMUSH, TinyMUX, TinyMUSH, TinyMUSE and RhostMUSH. Other kinds of game do not get it: there is no button, Cmd-E does nothing, and /edit answers "no such command".

SquatClient finds out what kind of game a world is by itself: it recognises the server's name (or, for Diku-style games, the classic "By what name do you wish to be known?" prompt) in the first lines the game prints, and after you log in it quietly asks the game for its version with version() and, if that does not name the server, @version (nothing appears in the output). A game that is not logged in yet is not detected yet, so the editor shows up a moment after you connect. If detection gets it wrong, or the game hides its version, set it yourself:
in the world's settings (Worlds, then Game type), which is remembered, or

with /gametype pennmush (or cobramush, tinymux, tinymush, rhostmush, tinymuse, mush for any other MU) for the current connection. Other kinds of game have types too (circlemud, rom, smaug, diku, lpmud, lambdamoo, evennia, muck, coldmud, coffeemud, ironrealms, custom), and other means none of these. They never get the Object Editor. /gametype alone shows the current type and /gametype auto detects it again.
/edit open the Object Editor and bring back the objects you had open
/edit #12/CMDENGAGE open object #12 and select the attribute CMDENGAGE
/edit me, /edit here open yourself, or the room you are in
/edit Nav Console open an object by name (the game finds it; use a #dbref if two match)
Cmd-E (Ctrl-E) switch between the terminal and the editor
the Object Editor button the same, from the top bar

/edit is handled by the window itself and is never sent to the game. Your connections keep running while you edit: switch back with Cmd-E, Escape or the Terminal button and everything that happened is in the output. Ctrl-E is the end-of-line key on the input line, so there it does not switch views; use Cmd-E, the button, or press Ctrl-E from anywhere else.
Top row: the connected worlds. Click one to switch world (Alt-1 to Alt-9 work too). Each world has its own set of open objects.

Second row: the objects open in that world, labelled Name (#12). A dot marks unsaved changes. Close a tab with its x or Cmd-W; drag tabs to reorder. The + asks for an object: #123, me, here or a name, optionally followed by /ATTRIBUTE.

Left: the attribute list with a filter box. A dot means modified, ! means the last save was refused, a padlock means read-only, + means a new attribute that is not saved yet. + new attribute adds one; it is created by its first save.
Right: the code editor for the selected attribute, with highlighting, bracket matching and a problems list. Every attribute you visit keeps its unsaved text and its undo history while you switch.
Bottom strip: the number of bracket problems, the object's owner, type and flags, whether you control it, and the game's last reply.
When you open an object the client asks the game whether you control it.
You do not control it: the object opens read-only with a notice. You can read, copy and compare, but Save is off and the editor will not accept typing.
The game could not say: you can edit, and a notice says the game will decide when you save.
A protected attribute (locked or safe) shows a padlock and opens read-only when the game reports it as protected. Otherwise the game's reply on save decides.
Press Save, Cmd-S (Ctrl-S), or Cmd-Shift-S to save every changed attribute of the object. Before it writes, the client reads the attribute again.

Someone changed it meanwhile: nothing is saved, and a dialog shows the game's version and yours side by side. Choose Overwrite (store yours), Reload theirs (drop your changes) or Keep editing (your next save then overwrites).
The game refuses: your text stays exactly as you typed it, a red notice shows the game's own words (for example Permission denied.), and Save stays available.
After a successful save the value is read back. You see Saved, or a warning if the game stored something different from what you sent.

Nothing the editor reads or writes appears in the output pane or in your command history.

Long softcode is easier to read indented. Expand and Collapse (also Cmd-Alt-] and Cmd-Alt-[) change only how it looks: what is sent to the game is always the collapsed single line, exactly as when you send a block from the command window. They never change what the code means.

Lines that start with / are commands; everything else is text for the game. A script is a plain text file (usually ending in .tf) of commands that you load with /load.
/set greeting=Hello /echo %greeting, world /def -t'* tells you: *' -ahCgreen tell = /echo Got a tell from %P1

A macro is a named list of commands made with /def. With -t it becomes a trigger that runs when matching text arrives from the game. With -h it becomes a hook that runs on an event such as connecting.
Variables are set with /set and read with %name or %{name}.

SquatClient is a new, independent implementation. It contains no TinyFugue code or help text. It follows TinyFugue's documented behaviour and was compared side by side with a real TinyFugue 5.2. Thank you to Ken Keys and the TinyFugue community; see About and credits.
Works the same the command syntax and nearly all commands, macros and triggers with all their options, substitution, expressions, most functions, the hooks, the editing keys and history
Different, on purpose safer expressions, deterministic trigger order, scripts never send text by accident, Go-style regular expressions, more colours

The command syntax and most commands: /def, /set, /let, /if, /while, /for, /eval, /test, /repeat, /quote, /load, /require and more.
Macro options -t -m -h -p -n -F -g -a -P -b -w -E -c, and glob, simple and regexp patterns.
The expression language, its operators and most functions, and the hook names.
The Emacs-style editing keys and the input history.
Inside expressions, %x and %1 are variable references and are never read again as text. That stops text from a game from sneaking commands into your scripts.
=~ and !~ compare strings exactly; =/ and !/ are glob matches. There is no % operator: use mod().
Triggers fire in a predictable order: by priority, then by definition order, and only one macro per priority unless you give -F. TinyFugue picks at random among equals.
Every wildcard of a glob trigger is available as %P1, %P2 and so on.
A script file that contains a line that is not a command is an error. Scripts never send text to a game by accident.
Backquote command substitution is not provided, because it meant running a shell.
Colour attributes also accept 256-colour numbers, the rgb cube, grayN and #rrggbb truecolour.
Every script run has a step limit, a time limit and nesting limits, so a runaway macro cannot freeze the client.
Regular expressions use the RE2 style: fast and safe, but without look-around or back-references.
Text is handled in whole characters, so strlen("é") is 1.
The complete list, with TinyFugue's behaviour next to SquatClient's, is in Differences from TinyFugue.

Short explanations of words used in this help and in MU games.
World: a saved connection to a game: its name, host, port and login. See Connecting and worlds.
Session: one live (or ended) connection. Each session has a tab.
Squatter: a small program (squatterd) on a server that keeps your sessions running while SquatClient is closed. See Squatter.
Direct: a world setting meaning the connection goes straight from your computer to the game and ends when the app closes.
Pairing: the one-time step that lets SquatClient talk to a squatter, confirmed with a fingerprint.
Fingerprint: a short code that identifies a squatter's encryption certificate. You compare it once while pairing.
Scrollback: the lines you can scroll back to.
Macro: a named list of commands made with /def. You run it by typing /name.
Trigger: a macro that runs automatically when a line from the game matches a pattern. See Macros: /def.
Hook: a macro that runs when an event happens, such as connecting or disconnecting.
Pattern: the text a trigger looks for. A glob pattern uses for any text and ? for one character. A regexp is a regular expression.
Variable: a named value you set with /set and read with %name.
Attribute (in scripts): the colour and style of text, such as bold or red. See Attributes.
Plugin: a Lua file that adds behaviour; see Lua scripting.
MU\: MUDs, MUSHes, MUXes, MOOs and similar text games.
MUSH: a kind of MU where players build objects and write programs in the game itself.
Softcode: the programs players write inside a MUSH, as opposed to the server's own code (hardcode).
dbref: the number that identifies every object in a MUSH, written with a hash sign, such as #123.
Attribute (in a MUSH): a named piece of text stored on an object, for example a description or a command. Not the same as a text attribute above.

It is designed so that most existing TinyFugue scripts run as written: the commands, macros, triggers, hooks and expressions work the way TinyFugue users expect.

It is a new, independent implementation. It contains no TinyFugue code, so a few things behave differently, and some things that only make sense in a terminal are not available. Everything that differs is listed in TinyFugue Script Compatibility. Thank you, Ken, and thank you to the TinyFugue community for decades of documentation, scripts and answers.
Scripts are plain text files (.tf). Everything below can be typed on the input line, put in a script and loaded with /load, or run by triggers and hooks.
A line that starts with / is a command. Any other line is text and is sent to the world (not expanded, unless /set sub=on).

A command line is split into statements at %; only (a plain ; is ordinary text, as in TinyFugue: /echo a;b prints a;b). Separators inside $[...], $(...) and %{...} do not split. /def, /repeat and /eval take the rest of the line, keeping %; unsplit so that it separates statements when their body runs later:
/def greet = /echo hello %; /echo again ; the whole body is stored
Trailing blanks before a %; are dropped.

Script files: blank lines and lines starting with ; are ignored; a line ending in \ continues on the next line (leading blanks of the next line are dropped). Every other line must be a command (non-command lines in a file are an error: a script never sends text by accident). Blocks (/if, /while, /do, /for) may span lines and are collected until their /endif / /done.
Errors print as % message and the script keeps going, except that an error inside a loop body ends the loop. At most 20 errors are shown per run.
Performed on the arguments of ordinary commands and on every statement of a macro body when it runs.
%name, %{name} variable (local first, then global); unset is empty
% all arguments as typed; %# their count; %0 the macro name
%PL %PR text left / right of the last regexp match; %L is the last positional parameter, %R a random one
%-N %{-N} %-L all parameters but the first N / but the last
%{sel-default} the default when the selector expands to nothing
%P0..%P9, %{P12} match parts: P0 the whole match, P1.. captures
%? return value of the last command or macro
%{?name} 1 if the variable is set, else 0 (extension)
${name} the body of macro name (an error if there is none)
\c \n the character c with no special meaning (\%, \$, \\); \65 / \0x41 / \0101 the character with that decimal / hex / octal code
$(command) what the command echoed (lines joined by spaces); if it echoed nothing, its /return value
Substitution is a single pass: substituted text is not rescanned, so text from the MUD can never inject commands through %. /eval expands its arguments and then runs the result, which expands again:
/set cmd=/echo hi /eval %cmd ; runs /echo hi /eval /echo %%{x} ; first pass leaves %{x}, second pass expands it
Triggers receive % = the line, %1.. = its words, %P0 = the whole match, %P1.. = glob wildcards or regexp groups in order, %PL/%PR for regexp triggers.

Values are integers (int64), floats, or strings. Text that looks like a number is a number. In arithmetic, text counts by its leading number: "12abc" 2 is 24 and plain words are 0. Truth: the numeric value is non-zero, so plain words and the empty string are false (as in TF). A float prints with 15 significant digits and, when it is a whole non-negative number, a trailing dot: pow(2,10) is 1024., 0.1+0.2 is 0.3 (TF output, verified). The on/off ("enumerated") variables such as gag read as 1/0 in an expression and on/off as text.
\ \ \ logical or (short-circuit; the value is the last operand evaluated; \ \ is an extension)
& && logical and (short-circuit; value of the last operand evaluated; && is an extension)

= == != < > <= >= =~ !~ =/ !/ one precedence level, left to right. =/==/!=/<.. compare numerically (leading-number coercion); when neither side starts with a number they compare as text (TF would call any two words equal). =~ !~ exact string equal / not equal (never numeric). =/ !/ glob match / no match (case-insensitive): str =/ "pat"
/ multiply, divide (integer division when both are integers; division by zero is an error)

Barewords are variables (x); name(args) calls a function; {x}, {1}, {}, {#} and %x, %1, %, %#, %{name} read variables and parameters without re-parsing the value as expression text (prefer these for script input). There is no % operator (use mod()); % is not interpolated inside string literals (use strcat). A $[expr] inside an expression is evaluated first (so /return $[1+2] works). String literals use " or ' with \n \t \r \e \\ \" escapes. Numbers: 12, 1.5, .5, 1e3, 0x1f (hex, x++ and x-- are extensions).
A user macro can be called like a function: /def add = /return {1} + {2} then $[add(2, 3)].
/set name=value (or /set name value) always sets a global (a local of the same name still shadows it while the macro runs). name := value in an expression assigns the nearest variable, else a global.
/let name=value creates/sets a local that lives until the macro returns. Locals are dynamically scoped: macros called from it can see them. A /for counter does not outlive its loop.
/setenv name=value is /set plus marking it exported; /export name marks an existing one. /unset name. /listvar [glob]. /set alone lists everything.
Names are [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]. Values are strings that act as numbers when numeric.

TF's on/off variables (gag hilite more wrap visual borg login ...) store on or off whatever you assign (1, 0, on, off). Their defaults are TinyFugue's own (checked against a real TinyFugue; see Variables).

Behavioural variables read by the interpreter: gag and hilite (off disables gag/hilite effects), matching (default /def match mode), hiliteattr (attribute used by /hilite, default B), sub (on expands % in typed text), quiet, ptime (default /repeat delay), wordpunct, TZ (UTC or a fixed offset such as UTC+2, -0530, used by ftime/mktime), visual (a layout switch handled by the app), histsize. Others from TinyFugue are accepted as ordinary variables.

The body is stored unexpanded and expanded each time the macro runs. Calling /name args runs it with %1.. set from args. A macro may also be a trigger, a hook, or a key binding. Options (no space between the letter and its value; quote values containing spaces with '..', ".." or {..}):
-t<pattern> trigger on received text matching the pattern
-m<glob\ simple\ regexp> pattern style (default glob, or $matching)
-h<HOOK [argpattern]> run when the hook fires (optional glob over the hook's arguments)
-n<shots> / -1 delete the macro after that many firings
-F fall-through: after firing, let lower-priority matches fire too
-a<attrs> highlight the whole line (see Attributes); g in the attrs gags (-g alone is an extension)
-P<n><attrs> highlight part n (0 whole match, 1..9 capture/wildcard)
-E<expr> extra condition; must be true for the macro to fire
-c<percent> fire with that probability (-c0 never; a macro that loses the roll is simply not a match)
-i invisible: not listed by /list, and /purge skips it unless given -i

glob matches the whole line, ignoring case: any text, ? one character, [a-z] / [^a-z] classes, {red|blue} whole-word alternatives (they must start at the beginning or after a space and end before a space or the end; alternatives may contain wildcards), \ a literal. Write dragon to match anywhere. Each wildcard becomes %P1...
simple: the line must equal the pattern exactly (case-sensitive).
substr: the line must contain the pattern.

regexp: Go (RE2) syntax, matches anywhere in the line, %P0.., %PL, %PR. As in TF a pattern with no upper-case letter matches case-insensitively. The positional parameters of any trigger are the words of the line.

Dispatch: matching macros are ordered by priority (high first), then definition order. The first one fires; if it has -F the next fires too, and so on. Only one macro per priority level fires unless -F is used (a deliberate simplification: TF picks randomly among equals; otherwise identical). A hook fires its macros the same way; hook arguments become %1...
/undefn N... remove by number shown in /list
/list [glob] list definitions in TF's format (% N: /def -p1 -mglob -t'..' name = body)
/purge [-i] [glob] remove all (or matching) visible macros; -i includes invisible ones
/enable name... /disable name... extension: switch a macro off/on without deleting it

/gag [pat [= body]] / /hilite [pat [= body]] / /partial regexp define a gag / -a$hiliteattr / partial-hilite trigger; with no argument /gag and /hilite turn the effect on; /nogag /nohilite remove or turn off
/trig pat = body, /trigp pri pat = body, /trigc pct pat = body, /trigpc pri pct pat = body define unnamed trigger macros
/hook EVENT[ pat] = body define a hook macro (/def -h); /unhook EVENT [pat], /untrig [-a..] pat, /undeft pat remove by exact pattern
/trigger [-gnl] [-w[world]] [-hEVENT] text run trigger (or hook) macros as if text had arrived; -n / -l list what would match instead
/dokey name editing actions (LEFT RIGHT HOME END WLEFT WRIGHT BSPC DCH BWORD DWORD DEOL DLINE) work on the input line and return the cursor; other actions are passed to the app
Redefining a name replaces the macro and fires the REDEF hook. A macro name shadows a built-in command of the same name; /builtin name args runs the built-in.
An attribute string is a comma-separated list; each item is flag letters optionally followed by one colour clause:
d i u s f r dim, italic, underline, strike, flash/blink, reverse

Colours: black red green yellow blue magenta cyan white (0-7), bright + name (8-15), a palette index 0..255 (xterm-256), rgbRGB (6x6x6 cube, digits 0-5, e.g. rgb530), gray0..gray23, and 24-bit #rrggbb or #rgb.
/echo -aCred,u red underlined /echo -aC196 palette 196 /echo -aC#ff8800,BC#001122 truecolour on truecolour /def -t'*dragon*' -ahC#ff4040 dragon /def -mregexp -t'(\d+) gold' -P1BCyellow,C0 gold
Inline markup (/echo -p, echo(), encodeattr): @{attrs} changes the current attributes (they accumulate; @{n} resets), @@ is a literal @: /echo -p @{Cred}red@{n} plain @{C#00ff00}green.

/if (expr) commands /elseif (expr) commands /else commands /endif /while (expr) ; /do directly after the header is optional ... /done /do ... /while (expr) /for var first last command ; TF form: one statement /for var first last commands /done ; block form /break /return [expr]
Commands after a header on the same line are the first statements of that body; separate statements with %; inside macro bodies:
(/let and /set store text: /let i=i+1 would store the string i+1; use $[...] to compute.)

In the TF form of /for the whole line is substituted once before the loop (exactly as in TinyFugue), so a body that wants the counter writes %%i (second pass) rather than %i; the counter is a local that vanishes after the loop. The block form (/done) substitutes per iteration. /do ... /while (expr) is an extension; TF's /while list /do list /done and /if list /then forms (a command list as the condition) are not available. A typed line closes unfinished blocks at its end; in a script file an unfinished block is an error. Every run is limited; see Limits and safety.
/help lists them and /help name prints usage.
Output: /echo [-w world] [-a attrs] [-p] text, /send [-w world] text, /beep, /notify title | body (extension), /gag, /hilite.

Processes: /repeat [-w[world]] [-n] [-<time>|-S] <count|i> <command> runs a command repeatedly (time is seconds, h:m or h:m:s; without a time $ptime (1 s) is used; -S runs it now, synchronously; -n runs the first one immediately); it returns the process id. /ps [-sr] [pid] lists processes in TF's table format, /kill pid... stops them.

/quote [-dsend|echo|exec] [prefix] 'file runs each line of a file (needs file access) and /quote [prefix] #command each line a command echoes; every line becomes prefix + line. Shell forms (!cmd, cmd ) are not available.
Worlds (need world access): /addworld [-Ttype] [-x] name [char pass] host port, /connect [world], /dc [world], /fg [world], /world name, /unworld, /listworlds [glob], /listsockets, /saveworld.

Display commands (handled by the app): /limit /unlimit /relimit /recall /log /localecho /statusadd /statusedit /statusrm /histsize. /input text inserts at the cursor of the input line; /suspend and the visual variable are passed to the app.

/restrict raises (never lowers) the restriction level: shell (always in force; there is no shell access), file (no /load /save /quote 'file /log), world (also no world/connection commands). SquatClient sets the initial level.

Strings: strlen strcat strcmp strncmp strchr strrchr strstr strrep substr pad tolower toupper replace substitute ascii char strcmpattr textencode textdecode (indices are in characters, 0 based and clamped; a negative index counts from the end (substr(s, -2) is the last two characters); strchr(s, set [, start]) is the first position of any character of set, or -1; tolower(s [, n]) only changes the first n characters; pad(s, w) right-justifies in w columns, a negative width left-justifies; replace(old, new, s) replaces every occurrence of old in s (TF argument order); substitute(text [, attrs [, inline]]) replaces the line being processed by a trigger).

Regexp: regmatch(pattern, string) returns the number of captured substrings including %P0 (0 when there is no match) and sets %P0..%P9, %PL, %PR for the rest of the macro. A pattern without upper-case letters is case-insensitive.
Math: abs sin cos tan asin acos atan exp ln log10 pow sqrt rand trunc mod (rand(n) is 0..n-1; rand(a, b) is inclusive; trunc and mod return integers; pow, sqrt and the rest return floats).

Time: time() (Unix seconds), mktime(y [,m [,d [,h [,mi [,s [,us]]]]]]), ftime(format [, secs]) (strftime codes %Y %y %m %d %e %H %I %M %S %p %a %A %b %B %j %Z %z %s %F %T %R %D %c %n %t %%), idle([world]) seconds since last input, sidle([world]) since last send.

Misc: eval(str) (expand and run as commands, returns the echoed text), test(expr), whatis(v) (int, float, string), getopts(optstring [, args]) (sets locals optx, returns the remaining arguments), echo(str [, attrs [, inline [, world]]]), send(str [, world]), prompt(str), worldinfo([world,] field) (name host port character type tls connected), isconnected([world]), isopen, fgworld(), nactive(), columns(), lines(), winlines(), isatty() (1), systype(), nlog() nmail() nread() morepaused() moresize() morescroll() getpid() gethostname() cputime() filename() (neutral values: no mail, no paging).

Input line (the app's input line; positions are characters): kbhead() kbtail() kbpoint() kblen() kbgoto(i) kbdel(i) kbmatch([i]) kbwordleft([i]) kbwordright([i]) kbcharback([n]) kbcharfwd([n]). Built-in commands can also be called as functions with one argument, e.g. repeat("-60 1 /echo hi").
Attributes: encodeattr(text, attrs), decodeattr(text) (markup to an ANSI string with 16/256/24-bit codes), stripattr(text) (remove markup and ANSI).

/def -hNAME [argpattern] name = body. Names: ACTIVITY ATCP BAMF BGTEXT BGTRIG CONFAIL CONFLICT CONNECT DISCONNECT GMCP ICONFAIL KILL LOAD LOADFAIL LOG LOGIN MAIL MORE NOMACRO OPTION102 PENDING PREACTIVITY PROCESS PROMPT PROXY REDEF RESIZE SEND SHADOW SHELL SIGHUP SIGTERM SIGUSR1 SIGUSR2 WORLD. SquatClient raises CONNECT DISCONNECT CONFAIL LOGIN WORLD SEND PROMPT ACTIVITY BGTEXT BGTRIG LOAD LOADFAIL REDEF RESIZE GMCP itself. The others can be defined, so scripts that use them still load, but nothing raises them. SEND fires just before text is sent (a SEND hook that sends does not trigger itself), LOAD and LOADFAIL fire around /load, and REDEF fires when a macro is redefined (arguments macro NAME; an identical redefinition is silent). /trigger -hNAME args fires a hook by hand; /hook NAME[ pat] = body defines one. Hook arguments are %1.., e.g. GMCP gets %1 = package, %2 = JSON. Hook names are fixed (an unknown name is an error).
Every top-level run (an input line, a received line, a hook, a key, a timer, one logical line of a loaded file) has:
a step budget (statements, loop iterations, expression evaluations, function calls; default 50 000),
a macro nesting limit (default 64) and file nesting limit (16),
a 256 KB cap on any one string value.

Exceeding a limit aborts that run with % script budget exceeded: ...; the interpreter stays usable. When a line is replayed (for example the lines you missed while detached from a squatter) no macro body runs, nothing is sent or notified, no shot is consumed and no variable is changed; only gag and highlight are computed.

; keep-alive every five minutes /def -hCONNECT on_connect = /repeat -300 100000 /send IDLE ; highlight tells and notify /def -mregexp -t'^(\w+) tells you: (.*)$' -P1Cbrightgreen,h tell = \ /notify Tell from %P1 | %P2 ; gag spam, but only from one world /def -wmain -t'\[Spam\]*' -g spam ; auto-loot with a condition and a 50% chance /def -t'* is dead.' -E'looting' -c50 loot = get all from corpse ; 256 and truecolour /def -t'*ALERT*' -a'BC#400000,C#ffe0e0,h' alert ; a helper with a return value /def max = /return {1} > {2} ? {1} : {2} /echo biggest: $[max(3, 9)]

SquatClient's scripting language is modelled on TinyFugue ("tf") and designed so that most existing TinyFugue scripts run as written. It is a new, independent implementation: it contains no TinyFugue code or help text, and it follows TinyFugue's documented behaviour. This reference lists, command by command, function by function, hook by hook and variable by variable, how each one compares. For a short overview read TinyFugue Script Compatibility first.

The behaviour was also checked side by side against a real TinyFugue 5.2: about 460 test lines in 39 groups. In 29 groups the results are identical; the other 10 differ only in the deliberate ways listed under Differences from TinyFugue.
Every entry in the tables below has one of these labels:
Matches tried against a real TinyFugue and gives the same result (apart from the listed differences)
Works implemented from the TinyFugue manual; not compared with a real TinyFugue
Partly works, with the limit stated
Not available yet not there yet: the command is accepted and ignored, or gives an error, as stated
Handled by the app SquatClient decides what it means (the window, the input line and so on)
Not applicable makes no sense in a graphical client
The rule behind all of this: match TinyFugue, unless TinyFugue's behaviour is a clear trap (for example, text from a game reaching expression source), and document every deliberate difference.

Expression substitution %x text substitution happens inside expressions Inside $[..], /if (..) etc. %x, %1, %, %{x} are variable references (never re-parsed as expression text); % is not interpolated in string literals. Removes a code-injection hazard from MUD text. $[..] nested inside an expression is supported (as TF).

Top-level lines a typed line or a script-file line is not substituted (only macro bodies and /eval are): /echo %x prints %x lines are substituted like a macro body, so /echo $[1+2] typed or in a file prints 3. Scripts that work in TF (they put logic in macros) behave the same.

== != < > .. on words numeric only, so any two non-numeric strings are "equal" ("abc" == "abd" is 1) numeric when either side starts with a number (identical to TF, including "12abc" == 12); plain text compared with plain text is compared as text. =~ !~ are the exact string forms in both.
Operators && \ \ x++ x-- 0x1f rejected (error) accepted extensions
Integers 32-bit-ish: results beyond that become reals (99999999993 prints 29999999997.) int64 arithmetic, wraps on overflow
Float text 0.1+0.2 prints 0.3; 1.03 is 3.; a literal keeps its text (1.0) same 15-digit format and trailing dot, except literals print normalised ($[1.0] is 1.)
Equal-priority triggers one chosen at random deterministic: priority desc, then definition order; the first fires (-F continues)
Glob captures %1.. are the words of the line %1.. are the words (as TF) and in addition %P1.. are the glob wildcards (%P0 the line)
Script files a non-command line is sent as text a non-command line in a loaded file is an error (no accidental sends); an unclosed block is an error
Error handling an error ends the macro errors are shown as % msg and the macro continues, except that an error inside a loop body ends the loop; at most 20 errors per run
/def of a built-in name CONFLICT hook message the macro shadows the built-in; /builtin cmd reaches the built-in
/set name = value stores = value (and warns) spaces around = are accepted
$(command) command substitution returns the echoed lines joined by spaces, else the /return value; backquote cmd is not available (it implied a shell)
After a failed substitution (${nosuchmacro}) the command still runs with an empty result the command is abandoned
/return with no value in a function call the call yields 0 yields the empty string
Strings byte strings (strlen("é") is 2) UTF-8 characters (strlen("é") is 1; substr, tolower etc. count characters)
strcmp strncmp difference of the first differing bytes (platform dependent) -1, 0 or 1
Regexps PCRE2 Go RE2: no look-around or back-references. regmatch() counts groups like TF and the caseless-if-no-capital rule is implemented.
whatis(x) looks at the unevaluated operand (decimal for a literal real, id:string for a variable) int, float, string of the value
winlines(), fgworld() lines()-1 (status line); empty with no socket the output pane height; the foreground world name
/list attribute letters lists a hilite as -aB lists it as written (-ah)
/trigger -h also displays the hook's default message runs the hook macros only
SEND hook not invoked by /send or send() unless enabled fired just before text is sent (does not recurse)
TZ system zones UTC and fixed offsets only
/do .. /while (e) not a TF construct accepted extension; TF's /while list /do list /done and /if list /then forms (a command list as condition) are not available
Budgets none every run has a step budget, wall deadline, nesting and string-size limits (see Limits and safety)
Colours 16/8 colours attribute strings also accept xterm-256 indices (C196), rgbRGB, gray0..23, truecolour #rrggbb; letters i (italic), s (strike) are additions; -g alone is a gag shorthand
Extensions /notify, /enable, /disable, /builtin, /return as a command, %{?name}, -E/-c on hooks

Where an early version disagreed with a real TinyFugue it was fixed, so these now behave as in TinyFugue: ; is plain text (only %; separates), = is equality (assignment is :=), &/| return the last operand, float formatting, leading-number coercion, text truthiness, replace() argument order (old, new, str), negative substr/strstr/strchr indexes, %L/%PL/%PR/%-N/%{sel-default}, backslash escapes, ${macro}, case-insensitive globs and whole-word {a|b}, [^..] only, regexps caseless without capitals, -msubstr, default priority 1, /for var a b command, dynamic scope of /let and global-only /set, /purge skipping invisible macros, /hook defining hooks, /trigpc defining a trigger, /ps format and /repeat semantics, regmatch() count, ascii("") is 0, mktime arguments.
What is not part of a graphical client

Only two families of TinyFugue features are left out on purpose: line wrapping (wrap wraplog wrapspace wrapsize) and paging (more morepaused morescroll moresize). Their variables exist (with TinyFugue's defaults) and are accepted and ignored, and the functions return neutral values (morepaused() is 0). SquatClient does its own wrapping and has a "pause when scrolled up" setting instead.
Everything else is supported, with a graphical meaning where needed:
Process commands /ps /kill /repeat (and /quote processes) Matches. /sh and /quote ! do not exist because there is no shell access; /restrict can also switch off file and world commands
Input-line functions and /input /dokey /bind Matches; they work on the app's input line

visual (split input/status layout), /dokey redraw, /suspend handled by the app (/suspend detaches squatter sessions; the others do nothing). /visual is not a command in TinyFugue either; visual is a variable

/core and the terminal signal hooks SIGHUP SIGTERM SIGUSR1 SIGUSR2 Not applicable (you can define them; they never fire)

SquatClient embeds Lua 5.1 as a sandboxed scripting language alongside the TinyFugue-style scripting language. Scripts are plain .lua files.
Everything lives in the global table squat. Each plugin gets its own global environment: globals you assign are private to your plugin, and changing string, table or math never affects other plugins.
All scripts run on one thread, one at a time. You never need locks.

Every call into your code (a trigger, a handler, a timer tick, loading the file) has a budget (about 5 million VM instructions and 500 ms wall-clock by default). Exceeding it aborts that call with an error in the log; the client keeps running and your other handlers still work.
Errors in one plugin never stop another plugin.

A line can be live (just arrived) or replayed (scrollback/backlog re-processed after reattaching). Replayed lines only get display effects: gag, highlight colours, and spans returned by line handlers. On replayed lines:
trigger fn callbacks are not called;

line/prompt handlers are called (with l.live == false) so they can restyle or gag, but squat.send, echo, notify, tf, var.set, var.del, after, timer, on, trigger, alias and remove do nothing and return false.
Write line handlers so they compute the display result from the text, and put side effects in trigger fns.

Available: base functions (pairs, pcall, error, setmetatable, tostring, unpack ...), string, table, math, coroutine, and a restricted os with only time, date, clock, difftime (using the client's clock). print(...) goes to the log.

Not available: io, debug, package, os.execute/remove/rename/getenv/exit, dofile, loadfile, string.dump, getfenv/setfenv, module, newproxy, native modules. loadstring/load work but compile into your own environment and refuse binary chunks. string.rep results are capped (4 MiB).
require("name") loads name.lua (dots become /) from your plugin's own directory only.
squat.send(text [, world]) Send a line to the game. Returns true, or nil, err.
squat.echo(x [, world]) Show text locally. x is a string, one span {s="..."}, or an array of spans/strings.
squat.log(text [, level]) Write to the client log; level is "info", "warn" or "error".
squat.world() Display name of the world the current line/event belongs to.
squat.now() Seconds since the Unix epoch (float) from the client clock.
world defaults to the world of the line/event being handled (timers remember the world they were created in). Calling send/echo/tf with no current world and no world argument is an error.
A span is a table: {s="text", fg=..., bg=..., b=true, dim=, i=, u=, st=, blink=, rev=, link="url"}.
fg/bg is an integer 0-255 (xterm-256 palette index; 0-15 follow the theme) or a string "#rrggbb" for 24-bit truecolor. Both survive the round trip to the display exactly; no quantisation.
prompt the same, only for flushed prompts
connect, disconnect {world, ...} (more fields depending on the event)
gmcp {package, data, raw, world} (data is the decoded JSON)
input {text, world}; return true to swallow the input
timer a table describing the tick
Line handlers may modify the line:
squat.on("line", function(l) if l.text:find("spam") then return {gag = true} end l.spans = {{s = "[!] ", fg = 196}, unpack(l.spans)} -- assign a new table (in-place edits are not seen) end)
Return {gag=true} to hide the line, {spans=...} to replace it, {stop=true} to stop later rules. A gag does not stop later rules (so a gagged line can still trigger an auto-heal).
Ordering: triggers and line handlers form one list, run by priority (higher first, default 0), then in registration order. This is deterministic and identical on live and replayed lines.
squat.on returns an id; squat.remove(id) (alias squat.cancel) unregisters it.

squat.trigger{ match = "You are hit by * for * damage.", -- glob unless regex=true regex = false, -- true: RE2 regular expression (unanchored search) icase = false, -- case-insensitive gag = false, -- hide the line (display effect, also on replay) fg = "#ff8800", bg = 17, b = true, u = true, -- highlight (display effect, also on replay) hilite = "line", -- "line" (default) or "match": colour only the matched text world = "MyMUSH", -- optional: only this world (name or id) priority = 0, fn = function(m) ... end, -- optional, live lines only }

Glob: matches the whole line; matches any run (captured), ? one character, \ and \? are literal. Regex: RE2 syntax (<https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax>): linear-time, no backreferences or lookaround; named groups (?P<name>...).
fn(m) gets m.text, m[0] (whole match), m[1..n] (captures; "" if a group did not take part), m.named.<name>, m.world, m.live, m.spans, m.prompt. It may return {gag=true}/{spans=...}/{stop=true}.
Aliases run on text the user typed:
squat.alias{match = "k *", fn = function(m) squat.send("kill " .. m[1]) end}
Same match options (regex, icase, world, priority). An alias handles the input (it is not sent) unless its function returns false; the first handling alias wins.
squat.timer{every = 30, count = 5, fn = function() ... end} -- count omitted: repeat forever squat.after(2.5, function() ... end) -- once local id = squat.timer{...}; squat.cancel(id)
Intervals are seconds (minimum 0.05 by default, at most 512 live timers). Timers are removed on plugin reload. A tick that errors is logged and the timer keeps going.

squat.var.get(name [, default]), squat.var.set(name, value), squat.var.del(name), squat.var.keys(). Values are strings, numbers, booleans, or tables of those (JSON-compatible; functions and cycles are rejected). set(name, nil) deletes. The store is shared by all plugins (prefix your names) and survives /reload.
squat.regex.match(pattern, text) returns nil or a table m[0], m[1..n], m.named; squat.regex.test(pattern, text) returns a boolean; squat.regex.replace(pattern, text, repl) uses $1/${name}.

squat.tf(code [, world]) runs one line of TinyFugue-style input (true or nil, err). Going the other way, the /lua <code> command runs Lua in a persistent console environment that keeps its globals between commands.

plugins/ heal.lua a single-file plugin named "heal" combat/ plugin.json {"name": "combat", "version": "1.0", "description": "...", "enabled": true, "main": "main.lua"} main.lua entry point (default main.lua, then init.lua) util.lua require("util")

plugin.json is optional; "enabled": false skips the plugin. A plugin that fails to load is reported and skipped. /reload discards all handlers, timers and plugin globals and re-runs every plugin from disk.

squat.trigger{ match = "^HP: (\\d+)/(\\d+)", regex = true, fn = function(m) local hp, max = tonumber(m[1]), tonumber(m[2]) if hp / max < 0.4 and squat.now() - squat.var.get("last_heal", 0) > 3 then squat.var.set("last_heal", squat.now()) squat.send("cast heal") end end, }
squat.trigger{match = "*tells you*", fg = "#ff8800", b = true} squat.trigger{match = "treasure", regex = true, hilite = "match", fg = "#ffd700", bg = 52}
Gag spam (still counting it on live lines):
squat.trigger{match = "^<Spam> ", regex = true, gag = true, fn = function() squat.var.set("spam_count", squat.var.get("spam_count", 0) + 1) end}
squat.on("connect", function() squat.timer{every = 300, fn = function() squat.send("") end} end)
squat.alias{match = "k *", fn = function(m) squat.send("kill " .. m[1]) end}
squat.trigger{match = "* arrives.", fn = function(m) squat.tf("/echo -aB Welcome, " .. m[1] .. "!") end}
Limits (what the budget can and cannot stop)

Enforced per call: VM instruction count (main thread), wall-clock timeout (also stops coroutines), heap-growth ceiling (sampled every 65536 instructions, process-wide so approximate), Lua call depth and stack size, string.rep size, timer/variable counts. Not interruptible: a single long-running built-in such as a pathological string.find pattern or very wide string.format; the call is marked failed when it returns, but it can still occupy the (single) script thread until then. Prefer squat.regex (RE2, linear time) for untrusted patterns.
